# As temperatures spike, this new report outlines humanity’s options for containing climate change 

Image credit Credit: Martin Levecoy/AFP 

Published on 21 Oct 2026 

The chance of holding global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels with no or limited overshoot – a key target of the Paris Agreement on climate change – is now gone. 

However, according to the Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return, published on 21 October by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), this overshoot need not be permanent. 

By dramatically reducing greenhouse gas emissions and removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, humanity can minimize peak temperatures and chart a path back to 1.5°C by the end of the century. This is the best remaining option for limiting the impact of climate change, the report found. 

“We’ve spent decades postponing cuts to emissions and now we’re facing the consequences,” says Anne Olhoff, the Director of the UNEP-Copenhagen Climate Centre. “The world can still attain the goals of the Paris Agreement but we must work hard to not only meet but surpass our most ambitious climate targets. The longer we wait, the larger the risk that we jeopardize the temperature goal.” 

Here’s a closer look at the main findings of the Emissions Gap Report 2026. 

We’re going to pass 1.5°C of warming, which is the most ambitious target of the Paris Agreement. What is the best possible scenario at this point? 

The report looks at the “lowest possible” 1.5°C overshoot scenario. In this scenario, humanity limits peak warming to 1.7-1.8°C by around the middle of the century and brings temperatures back down to or below 1.5°C. This would require sustained emissions cuts plus carbon dioxide removal. 

To return to 1.5°C of warming by 2100, the world will need to cut greenhouse gas emissions by nearly 70 percent within the next decade-and-a-half

What do we need to do to return to 1.5°C of warming by the end of the century? 

Achieving that goal won’t be easy. It means immediate and aggressive cuts to greenhouse gas emissions, reducing them by 18 per cent by 2030, 45 per cent by 2035 and 69 per cent by 2040. 

This means annual reduction rates of nearly 6 per cent from 2025 to 2035 – more strenuous cuts than those laid out in the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s most recent assessment report. 

But if countries start this year and follow this trajectory, there is a 50 per cent chance of returning to 1.5°C by 2100, the report found. 

Urgent action is crucial; every five years of carbon dioxide emissions at current levels will push warming up by around 0.1°C. 

Would limiting the overshoot of the 1.5°C target spare us from the effects of climate change? 

No. Achieving this doesn’t mean we avoid the negative impacts of climate change, which can include everything from droughts to floods to more frequent superstorms. But it would help minimize them. Plus, every additional year of warming above 1.5°C raises the risk of severe and irreversible changes, with catastrophic implications for humanity. These include changes in ice sheets, permafrost carbon, ocean circulation and corals. 

What has to happen for the world to reach the lowest-possible overshoot scenario? 

Attaining the global emissions cuts outlined above would require extending already ambitious sectoral targets laid out in the first Global Stocktake under the Paris Agreement. 

By 2035, renewable electricity capacity would need to triple, and the share of coal in our energy supply would need to drop by over half. Emissions of methane – a powerful greenhouse gas – would have to come down by 25 per cent, all compared with 2025 levels. 

Global greenhouse gas emissions have marched steadily upwards since 1990, putting in jeopardy the Paris Agreement goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 °C above pre-industrial times.

How far off are we from the goals of the Paris Agreement? 

If we continue with business as usual, we have no hope of achieving the 1.5°C target. Under current government policies, warming would reach 2.8°C by the end of the century, a number widely considered disastrous. And the temperature rise wouldn’t stop there. 

If countries made good on all their commitments under the Paris Agreement, that would nudge warming down a little, to a still-sweltering 2.6°C. If, in addition, countries made good on their so-called net-zero targets, warming could be limited to 2.1°C. But even this lower temperature is well above what countries agreed to in the Paris Agreement. 

How can carbon dioxide removal help bring temperatures back down? 

To have any chance of returning to or below 1.5°C, the world can no longer rely on emissions cuts alone. Countries must also actively remove and permanently store carbon dioxide — around 320 gigatonnes of it by the end of the century. 

However, this option is fraught with uncertainty. Carbon dioxide removal comes with a host of socioeconomic and technological challenges, including the use of expensive and unproven technology. 

And while carbon dioxide removal is an important tool, it should never be considered a substitute for emissions reductions, the report says. There are limits to how much carbon can be stored, which again points to an urgent need for fast and deep emission cuts to minimize peak temperatures. 

Global greenhouse gas emissions have marched steadily upwards since 1990, putting in jeopardy the Paris Agreement goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 °C above pre-industrial times

What kind of progress have we made on renewable energy since the Paris Agreement? 

Renewable energy has become increasingly popular since the Paris Agreement was adopted in 2015. 

The deployment of solar photovoltaic panels that convert sunlight into electricity in particular has been astonishing, growing a whopping seven times faster than anticipated. As well, the expansion of wind farms has outpaced even the most optimistic forecasts. 

All of this is a sign that this sector, at least, is moving in the right direction. If additional policies are put in place to support this trend, we could triple renewable capacity by 2030, bringing solar and wind energy in line with the lowest possible overshoot scenario. 

How are we doing in reducing emissions from other sectors? 

Although progress on renewable energy has been promising, the report finds other sectors are lagging. 

Global emissions have risen 0.8 per cent a year on average over the past decade. Although they were roughly the same in 2025 as in 2024, it is too early to say they have peaked. 

In 2025, carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels rose (carbon dioxide is by far the most common greenhouse gas). Methane emissions stayed the same. 

How effective have our current climate policies been in reducing emissions? 

Despite these trends, there is evidence that climate policies across the globe have had a real impact on reducing emissions. 

The report identifies 63 structural changes – ranging from investments in renewable energy to the imposition of carbon taxes – that have helped bring down emissions significantly. 

Following the lowest possible overshoot scenario requires replicating policies like these globally, and across all sectors of the economy, says UNEP’s Olhoff. 

“Every year spent in a warmer world raises the risk of irreversible damage to the planetary systems that sustain us,” she said. “Unless we quickly cut greenhouse gas emissions, our best chance for avoiding a full-blown climate catastrophe will disappear in the rearview mirror.”
